EFW and Infant Mortality: Preliminary Analysis

Propensity Score Matching Estimates of Major Changes in Economic Freedom

Author

Geloso & Wilhelm

Published

May 7, 2026

1 Introduction

This is a preliminary analysis of the causal effect of large, sustained changes in economic freedom (EFW) on infant mortality outcomes (IM). The methodology draws from Callais & Young (2023) and Grier (2025), extending their propensity-score matching framework to infant mortality. I also include two measures that assess changes in the statistical uncertainty of each country’s estimates for IM: confidence interval (con_int = upper_limit - lower_limit) and relative precision (rp = [con_int/2]/IM).

This analysis forms the basis for two papers:

  1. EFW changes on IM

  2. EFW changes on estimate precision as a proxy for “state capacity” (other than the “size and scope of government” hokum)

I introduce two new methods to the “change in EFW” treatment effects that I didn’t see in the EFW treatment literature:

  1. Examine EFW score drops. \(\leftarrow\) seems more symmetrical and we’d expect to see changes in the corresponding (but opposite) direction. This examines the “liberalism failures” as well as the successes.

  2. Examine EFW rank changes. \(\leftarrow\) I’ve seen a lot of comments/push-back on the validity of the EFW index score. Changes to the relative rank of a country short-circuits reviewer comments overly concerned with “EFW data issues”. Changes in relative rank will not capture changes in secular, worldwide trends towards more liberalisation. This analysis can “be in our back pocket” if we encounter such a reviewer.

Outcomes (5-year periods):

  1. \(\Delta\text{IM}\) — change in infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births)
  2. \(\Delta\text{con\_int}\) — change in confidence interval width (\(\text{IM\_upper} - \text{IM\_lower}\))
  3. \(\Delta\text{rp}\) — change in relative precision \(= (\text{con\_int}/2)\,/\,\text{IM}\)

For \(\Delta\text{IM}\), a negative ATT indicates a sustained EFW liberalisation event is associated with a larger decline in infant mortality among treated countries.

3 Definitions of EFW Treatments

We identify four types of EFW events in a 5-year panel from 1970 to 2015. Treatments are constructed in 1) Import_Merge.R and grouped by economic interpretation:

Group Treatment Definition Interpretation
A EFW Score Jump EFW index rose \(\geq +1.0\) point over 5 years Liberalisation
A EFW Rank Drop EFW rank improved \(\geq 17\) places (lower rank = more free) Liberalisation
B EFW Score Drop EFW index fell \(\leq -1.0\) point over 5 years Restriction
B EFW Rank Jump EFW rank worsened \(\geq 17\) places Restriction
Note

We can modify the “rank change” cutoff to identify treatment. I chose 17 because there are 162 countries in EFW. A 1/10th change is equivalent to a change in relative rankings by 162/10 rounded up.

A rise in EFW score corresponds to a fall in rank (Rank 1 = most free). Group A and Group B identify the same underlying directional change, measured two ways: 1) Changes in Index Score and 2) Changes in Relative Rank.

Observations adjacent to any qualifying event within the same country are set to NA (lag 1, lag 2, lead 1) to avoid contamination from overlapping reform episodes (Callais & Young 2023). Venezuela 2000 is excluded as a structural break. (I follow Callais & Young exaclty here. We can alter accordingly if you see fit.)

4 PSM Methodology

4.1 Three Matching Estimators

For each treatment \(\times\) outcome combination we estimate the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) using three matching specifications. All three condition on the same vector of pre-treatment covariates (see Covariates below). Differences across the three estimators provide a robustness check; agreement across them strengthens the causal interpretation.

4.1.1 1. PSM — 3 Nearest Neighbors (NN3)

A logistic regression of the binary treatment on the covariate vector produces a propensity score for each observation. Each treated unit is then matched to its 3 nearest control units on the propensity score within a caliper of 0.25 standard deviations (Austin 2011). Matching is done without replacement: each control unit can serve as a match for only one treated unit. The ATT is the average outcome difference between treated units and their matched controls. Standard errors are computed by non-parametric bootstrap (200 replications, seed 50726).

4.1.2 2. PSM — Epanechnikov Kernel

Same logit-based propensity score as NN3, but each treated unit is compared to a weighted average of all control units, where the weights follow an Epanechnikov kernel function (declining smoothly with PS distance). This estimator uses information from many controls per treated unit, trading some variance reduction for reliance on the kernel specification. Standard errors by bootstrap (200 replications).

4.1.3 3. Mahalanobis NN3 with Bias Adjustment

Skips the propensity-score model entirely. Each treated unit is matched to its 3 nearest controls in the full covariate space using Mahalanobis distance (which accounts for covariance among covariates)1. An Abadie-Imbens (2011) bias correction is applied via regression adjustment. Standard errors are computed analytically. Matching is done with replacement, so a strong control unit can match several treated units.

4.2 Covariates

Each treatment regression conditions on the following pre-treatment covariates (all lagged one 5-year period to ensure measurement before the treatment event, following Callais & Young 2023 and the existing Stata pipeline Results_DecileGrowth5yr.do)2:

Covariate Description Source
lagEFW EFW summary index (lagged) Fraser Institute

Warning

Covariates listed above may be subject to change. See “Caveats” below.

5 PSM Results

ATT estimates with bootstrap standard errors (200 replications, seed 50726) for the two PSM estimators, and with analytic Abadie-Imbens standard errors for the Mahalanobis estimator. Significance stars: * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.

A negative ATT for \(\Delta\text{IM}\) indicates that treated countries saw a larger decline in infant mortality than comparable untreated countries — a beneficial effect.

6 Balance & Distribution Diagnostics

Balance diagnostics restricted to the two outcomes specified in the analysis brief: Infant Mortality Rate (\(\Delta\text{IM}\)) and Relative Precision (\(\Delta\text{rp}\)). For each treatment we show:

  1. Propensity-score density plot — kernel density of the estimated propensity score for treated and control units, before vs after PSM NN3 matching. Better overlap on the right panel = better matched-sample comparability.
  2. Love plot — standardized mean differences (SMDs) for each PSM covariate, before vs after matching. Dashed reference lines at \(\pm 0.10\) mark the threshold below which a covariate is conventionally considered well balanced (Austin 2011).

7 Caveats

WarningCaveats
  • Years covered. The current sample spans 1970–2015, solely relying on the Callais & Young covariate panel. Extending through 2023/24 will require sourcing more recent versions of the underlying covariate series (PWT, WDI, Polity5). The covariates we select may change and need to be updated.
  • EFW & IM data. The Fraser Institute EFW Index 2025 edition (covering 1970–2023) and the UN IGME Infant Mortality Rate dataset used here are the latest and greatest publicly available data.
  • Covariates. The propensity-score covariates in this analysis are taken directly from Callais & Young (2023). To exploit the full 1970–2023 EFW window, the covariates we deem most relevant need to be updated and extended through 2023/24 (and potentially expanded to include health-specific controls relevant to the infant-mortality outcome).
  • Fertility Rate. A country’s fertility rate likely has a more direct endogenous relationship with infant mortality. We need to be careful about how fertility rate fits in our specification and identification strategy. Naively including it in our basket of PSM covariates seems to be moving the difference in means (between treated and control groups) in the unbalanced direction.

8 Questions and Considerations for Vincent

  1. Do you want to include drops in EFW scores? If yes, this means we’ll have two different treatment groups. I assume both the treated jumps and drops should be removed from the control group before matching and balancing?
  2. Do you want to include changes in relative rank? This can be straightforwardly done in the analysis, but we may not want to include them in the papers we submit?
  3. You mentioned the Statistical Performance Indicators database SPI This series only goes back to 2016. The legacy Statistical Capacity Index SCI has coverage from 2003-2020. This could potentially overlap with four of the (5-year) periods in our panel. Let me know if/how you would like to use this as a point of comparison for the “statistical estimate quality” paper.

9 References

Austin, Peter C. “An introduction to propensity score methods for reducing the effects of confounding in observational studies.” Multivariate behavioral research 46.3 (2011): 399-424.

Callais, Justin T., and Andrew T. Young. “A rising tide that lifts all boats: An analysis of economic freedom and inequality using matching methods.” Journal of Comparative Economics 51.3 (2023): 744-777.

Grier, Robin. “The causal effect of economic freedom on female employment & education.” Contemporary Economic Policy 43.4 (2025): 698-713.
